Biography

Capt. George Symonette: Master Mariner of Inagua

Captain George Symonette remains one of the most remarkable, if often underappreciated, figures in the maritime history of the Bahamian archipelago. Recognized primarily as a veteran of the Inagua inter-island trade, Symonette’s life was inextricably bound to the sea and the vast salt pans of Great Inagua. As a master mariner, he not only commanded vessels across the treacherous waters of the Bahamas but also maintained the vital trade links that connected the southern Bahamian islands with the broader Caribbean network. His legacy is one of resilience, navigational brilliance, and an unwavering commitment to the economic survival of his island home during a period when salt was truly the white gold of the region.

Early Life on the Salt Island

Great Inagua, the southernmost island of the Bahamas, is a rugged, sun-baked land famous for its large populations of West Indian flamingos and its expansive salt ponds. Born into this harsh yet beautiful environment in the late 19th century, George Symonette grew up in Matthew Town, a settlement that owed its very existence to the ocean and the salt it yielded. In those days, long before the industrial-scale mechanization introduced by the Erickson family in the 1930s or the eventual takeover by Morton Salt, salt raking was a grueling, labor-intensive process. Families worked in the glaring sun, harvesting the crystallized sea salt by hand.

From an early age, Symonette was drawn less to the blistering heat of the salt pans and more to the cooling breezes of the sea. The salt had to be exported, and that required ships. The maritime culture of Inagua was robust; young boys learned to read the wind and the tides before they could read books. Symonette began his maritime apprenticeship on local sloops—small, agile vessels that navigated the shallow banks of the Bahamas. It was here that he learned the intricate art of seamanship, mastering the complex currents, sudden squalls, and hidden coral reefs that characterized the Bahamian waters.

Rise to Master Mariner

Symonette’s natural aptitude for navigation and leadership quickly set him apart from his peers. By his mid-twenties, he had earned his master mariner’s ticket, a prestigious accomplishment that commanded deep respect in the seafaring communities of the Caribbean. Earning this title meant he was legally and practically qualified to command a large merchant vessel, taking responsibility for the ship, its cargo, and the lives of its crew.

He soon took command of a large schooner, specifically designed for the heavy and bulky cargo of sea salt. These vessels were the lifeblood of Inagua’s economy. A master mariner from the Bahamas was required to be a jack-of-all-trades: a skilled navigator, a strict disciplinarian, an astute businessman, and a weather forecaster capable of smelling a hurricane before the barometer even dropped.

"To sail out of Inagua with a hold full of salt is to carry the sweat of your neighbors across the sea. A captain bears not just cargo, but the livelihood of his island." — Capt. George Symonette

The Caribbean Salt Trade

The period during which Captain Symonette operated was one where salt was of paramount importance. In an era before widespread electrical refrigeration, salt was the primary method for preserving fish, meat, and other perishable goods across the Caribbean and the Americas. The salt produced in Inagua was prized for its purity, the result of the island's unique combination of constant trade winds and high solar evaporation rates.

Symonette’s trade routes were extensive. He did not merely sail the protected waters of the Bahamian archipelago. He ventured out into the open Atlantic and the deeper, often tempestuous waters of the wider Caribbean. His manifest typically showed voyages to Jamaica, Cuba, Hispaniola, and the Turks and Caicos Islands.

In Jamaica, Inagua salt was traded for sugar, rum, and manufactured goods. In Cuba, it found a ready market in the bustling ports of Havana and Santiago de Cuba. Symonette was known for his sharp negotiating skills. He wasn't just delivering a commodity; he was acting as a merchant ambassador for Inagua. He understood market fluctuations, knew when to hold out for a better price, and knew which ports offered the most favorable terms of trade. His success brought considerable wealth back to Matthew Town, funding the construction of sturdy homes and supporting the local economy during lean years when the salt harvest was poor due to unseasonal rains.

Navigating Hurricanes and Hardships

The life of a Bahamian mariner was fraught with peril. The Caribbean is infamous for its hurricane season, and during Symonette’s era, there were no satellite forecasts or radio warnings to rely upon. A captain had to rely on his knowledge of the sky, the behavior of the birds, and the feel of the ocean swell.

Captain Symonette’s reputation was cemented during the Great Bahamas Hurricane of 1929. Caught in the open sea between Inagua and Jamaica, his schooner was battered by ferocious winds and monstrous waves. Legend has it that he lashed himself to the helm, staying on deck for two days and two nights, steering the ship through the worst of the tempest. He managed to bring his vessel and his entire crew safely back to port, though the ship suffered significant damage. This display of extraordinary endurance and seamanship made him a revered figure among his peers.

Beyond the natural dangers, there were economic hardships. The inter-island trade was subject to the whims of the global economy. When tariffs were raised by neighboring nations, or when steamships began to encroach on the traditional sail routes, Symonette had to adapt. He diversified his cargo, occasionally transporting timber, agricultural produce, and even mail, ensuring his vessel remained profitable and his crew employed.

Connectivity and Cultural Exchange

Perhaps Captain Symonette’s most significant contribution was the connectivity he fostered. Inagua, by virtue of its geographic location, is physically isolated from the Bahamian capital of Nassau, lying closer to Cuba and Haiti. Symonette’s regular voyages ensured that Inagua did not become culturally or economically marooned.

He brought back news from the wider world—newspapers from Kingston, political gossip from Havana, and the latest records that would influence local Bahamian music, inspiring future musicians like Blind Blake and other prominent Bahamian entertainers. His ship was a floating conduit for Caribbean culture. Furthermore, he often transported people—migrant workers seeking employment, families visiting relatives across the islands, and sometimes even political figures. Through his work, he wove the disparate islands of the Caribbean a little closer together.

"The sea does not divide us; it is the road that connects us. A ship is simply a cart upon that road, and I am merely its driver." — Capt. George Symonette

Later Years and Lasting Legacy

As the 20th century progressed, the maritime world began to change irrevocably. The graceful sailing schooners were gradually replaced by diesel-powered freighters. While Symonette adapted to these changes, his heart always belonged to the age of sail. He eventually retired to Matthew Town, becoming an elder statesman of the community.

In his later years, he dedicated himself to teaching the younger generation. He passed down the old ways of navigation by the stars and the traditional methods of reading the weather. He was a living repository of Inagua's history, frequently consulted by local leaders and historians.

Captain George Symonette passed away, leaving behind a legacy that is etched into the very fabric of Inagua's maritime identity. Today, he is remembered not just as a successful merchant or a skilled sailor, but as a crucial pillar of the Inaguan community. His life exemplifies the resilience, resourcefulness, and adventurous spirit of the Bahamian people. In an era when the sea was a formidable barrier, he made it a bridge, carrying the literal and metaphorical flavor of his island to the rest of the world.

Major Contributions

  • Captain George Symonette's major contributions lie in his pivotal role in sustaining the Inagua salt trade during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
  • By expertly navigating his schooners across the Caribbean, he ensured the economic viability of Great Inagua, exporting its primary resource, salt, to markets in Jamaica, Cuba, and Hispaniola.
  • Beyond economics, Symonette was instrumental in fostering regional connectivity.
  • His voyages served as vital communication and cultural links between the isolated Bahamian island and the broader Caribbean.
  • By transporting goods, mail, people, and news, he maintained Inagua's integration into the regional network, laying the groundwork for the island's modern maritime heritage.
